chunks.text: The most 80s of all of his games was OutRun, which provided the player with a glimpse of the luxurious jet-set lifestyle. OutRun was a quantum leap in visual and audio spectacle compared to the games early in the decade. Thanks to the ever-dropping prices of computer chips, the game was powered by the next generation in processors. The 16-bit CPU made it possible to calculate the positions of large numbers of sprites. The advanced video circuit also housed some impressive features.

It was not only able to display large numbers of sprites, but also store multiple background layers inside its video memory. Backgrounds could scroll individually to recreate a true parallax scrolling effect. Another major improvement was the sheer number of colors, allowing the artists to create lush scenery with sweeping sunsets.

chunks.text: Most games are made by development studios that have multiple people working on the same game, and AAA titles can even go into hundreds of developers, while small indie teams consist of at least two developers more often than not. However, it's very rare to encounter a bigger sized game where every single part is made by only one person. This is exactly the case with Stardew Valley though, since all the art, music, sound effects, dialogue and programming were done by

Eric Barone, also known as Concerned Ape. In 2011, Eric graduated from the University of Washington Tacoma with a computer science degree, so afterwards he applied at a few places, did some interviews, but they never offered him the job. At that point he didn't really know what to do next. Eric has always been into video games, drawing doodles, making music and writing, but he hadn't really considered combining all his hobbies to become an actual game developer.
Now that he was looking for a job, he decided to give it a shot and develop his first game. Eric figured he could get better at programming this way and improve his chances at scoring a job.

Like the most extreme example would be Silksong. They didn't release a demo. I mean, they didn't even give press copies. But I bet a huge chunk of people were going to play that game day one, no matter what. A bit of an extreme example, so consider Choo Choo Charles. I mean, the trailer went crazy. I knew several people who decided that they were going to play the game just based on that

So I was thinking, theoretically, if some people decide to buy a game before playing it, then a pitch deck would simulate a similar experience. So we tried this with Get to Work and it was truly eye-opening. Let me walk you through it. First, we have a brainstorm process where we find cool ideas and vote on our favorites. And during this process, we use our experience, we consider if it's something we can actually make, we look at the market research and genre and some other factors like whether it's appealing and does it have a strong fantasy. And from that, we pick the top seven ideas

and attempt to explain the game's loop. Some ideas just kind of fall apart. It's not clear how we would play, but the strong ones live on. And here we expand upon the ideas and create pitch decks. The first time I did it, I shared it with some friends and family. And even amongst a small group, the results were shocking. People didn't get bogged down by bugs or mechanics. I mean, there wasn't any, but they were able to focus on the idea. It simulated the first part of the purchasing experience.

chunks.text: And we'll start with this one. Yeah, that's right. We can take an existing game and use that as a jumping off point to make something new. For instance, we could take a game and move it into another perspective, like how Satisfactory began with the idea to move Factorio into first person. Or we could shift a game into a different theme or context, like how Subnautica's initial pitch was Minecraft, but underwater. We could move a game into a different medium.

Among Us, famously, is based on real-world social games like Werewolf. Or we could bring a game back from the dead. Stardew Valley was made simply because designer Eric Barone thought the Harvest Moon series had gotten progressively worse since the PS1 and was in desperate need of a better game. Of course, none of these games are simply re-skinned clones of those existing titles. They might use an existing game as a jumping-off point, but then

Then they'll get to explore the unique design space that comes from changing the perspective, world, medium, or whatever. A game will also change when fed through your unique perspective and set of influences.

chunks.text: overwhelming in an open world game. And that was partly the reason behind Nintendo creating the triangle rule. You see, Nintendo designed the terrain and landscape of Hyrule to be mostly made up of triangles. It's all hills, mountains, and rock formations that are shaped like pyramids and cones. And this has various benefits for the world design. Like, whenever you face a giant mountain, players get to decide whether to scale it or go around it, creating decision-making during exploration.

Also, the player's eye is naturally guided to the tip of the triangle, so you can place points of interest at the peak to draw the player closer. But most importantly, these triangles simply block whatever's behind, meaning that the player is rarely overwhelmed by a massive field of things to do. There's usually only a couple attractive places on screen, and the rest is hidden behind hills and mountains. But as you go towards these mountains, whatever's behind is gradually revealed. Whether you climb the hill,

try to move alongside it, more terrain will start to be shown. And this has an interesting outcome. It creates a constant source of surprise and curiosity as new locations make themselves known. So you might be going towards one landmark, but as you travel there, two or three new places are revealed. Perhaps a shrine on the horizon, or an enemy camp around a corner, or a distinctive looking rock, or a curious sight at the peak of a mountain. Wherever you go, and whatever you do, you'll be given

a few new things to catch your eye and attract you. Perhaps that new landmark will distract you, and you'll ditch your old plan and go somewhere new instead. When you're finished, you'll remember where you were supposed to go and head back there. Only to be distracted again. Whatever the case, this creates a chain reaction. An infinite loop of discoveries. A breadcrumb trail of landmarks. All of which makes you slowly move across the map, in an addictive quest of, ooh, what's that?
What's that? Ooh, what's that? And before you know it, you're at a Sheikah Tower, which is exactly where Nintendo wanted you to go in the first place.

chunks.text: Demo dominance. All right, so here's just a game. I'm going to show a lot of examples that are just awesome. Okay. Eden Crafters releases a demo and their wish lists go crazy. That big flatline, that's when they try the social media, the Reddit posting, nothing really works until you release a demo. Here's Parcel Simulator. Nothing really worked. Then he released
a demo and he got 17,000 wishlists. In one week, he got as many wishlists as he did for an entire two years before that place. You have to release a demo.

chunks.text: Try to come up with unique gameplay ideas and mechanics. This is one of the best ways to stand out, especially as an indie dev. Don't be afraid to share your ideas with other people. They will give you helpful feedback, and honestly, no one is interested in stealing your idea, because everyone thinks they have the best idea. Also, good execution is often more important than the idea itself.

chunks.text: This mentality was John Romero and id Software, the creators of Doom. These guys were animals back in the day. John Romero stated in his book that Carmack, Tom, and I had each been making games for 10 years before we started working together. It was another few years before we made Doom, and that was my 90th game. It's incredible that John made 90 games before working on Doom. But what is more interesting is that it took almost 15 years before John and his team found global success. So when asked about his success, John Romero said this,

Execution is everything. Success is not defined by an idea. It is determined by your ability to execute on that idea. Give yourself time to get good and don't be dissuaded by setbacks. Game development is like gameplay. Load your save and try again.

chunks.text: So you've chosen an engine, you've messed with it here and there, but you actually want to start making stuff. At this point, I would recommend to make extremely simple projects. When I was starting out, I would make really basic platformers, or make projects with singular mechanics like figuring out how to make bullets, how to make enemies, inventory systems, etc. Some developers would also recommend recreating classic games such as Pong or Space Invaders, and I do think this is a good idea. I encourage you to look at plenty of tutorials at this point too.
